question: A consolidated-drained triaxial test was conducted on a normally consolidated clay yielding the following data: σ₃ = 250 kN/m²; σ_d = 275 kN/m². Determine: (i) The angle of friction, (ii) Angle which the failure plane makes with the major principal plane, (iii) Normal stress and shear stress on the failure plane, (iv) Normal stress on the plane of τ_max.
solution:
Given Parameters:
Normally consolidated clay ⇒ c' = 0.
Confining stress σ'₃ = 250 kPa, Deviator stress σ_d = 275 kPa.
Major principal stress: σ'₁ = σ'₃ + σ_d = 250 + 275 = 525 kPa.
(i) Angle of Friction (φ'):
From Mohr-Coulomb for c = 0:
sin φ' = (σ'₁ - σ'₃) / (σ'₁ + σ'₃) = 275 / (525 + 250) = 275 / 775 = 0.3548.
φ' = arcsin(0.3548) = 20.78°.
(ii) Failure Plane Angle with Major Principal Plane (θ):
θ = 45° + φ'/2 = 45° + 10.39° = 55.39°.
(iii) Stresses on Failure Plane:
σ_f = [(σ'₁+σ'₃)/2] + [(σ'₁-σ'₃)/2] · cos 2θ = 387.5 + 137.5 · cos(110.78°) = 387.5 + 137.5(-0.3548) = 387.5 - 48.78 = 338.72 kPa.
τ_f = [(σ'₁-σ'₃)/2] · sin 2θ = 137.5 · sin(110.78°) = 137.5(0.9350) = 128.56 kPa.
(Check: τ_f / σ_f = 128.56 / 338.72 = 0.3795 = tan 20.78° ✓).
(iv) Normal Stress on the Plane of τmax:
The plane of maximum shear stress occurs at 2θ = 90° (θ = 45°):
σ = (σ'₁ + σ'₃) / 2 = (525 + 250) / 2 = 387.5 kPa (with τmax = 137.5 kPa).

topic: Infinite Slope Stability in Granular Soil with Seepage & Water Table Numerical
question: A granular soil has G = 2.70, e = 0.5 and φ = 35°. A slope has to be made of this material. If a factor of safety of 1.15 is needed against failure, determine the safe angle of slope when: (i) The slope is dry or submerged without seepage, (ii) If seepage occurs at and parallel to the surface of the slope, (iii) If seepage occurs parallel to the slope with the water table at a depth of 1.5 m, what is the factor of safety available on a slip plane parallel to the ground surface at a depth of 4 m. Assume slope angle is 30°.
solution:
Soil Parameters: G = 2.70, e = 0.5, φ = 35°, c = 0.
γsat = [(G + e)/(1 + e)] · γw = [(2.7 + 0.5)/1.5] × 9.81 = 20.93 kN/m³.
γ' = γsat - γw = 20.93 - 9.81 = 11.12 kN/m³.
γd = [G / (1 + e)] · γw = (2.7/1.5) × 9.81 = 17.66 kN/m³.
(i) Dry or Submerged without Seepage:
FS = tan φ / tan β ⇒ 1.15 = tan 35° / tan β ⇒ tan β = 0.7002 / 1.15 = 0.6089.
Safe slope angle β = arctan(0.6089) = 31.34°.
(ii) Seepage Parallel to Surface at Ground Level:
FS = (γ' / γsat) · (tan φ / tan β).
1.15 = (11.12 / 20.93) · (0.7002 / tan β) = 0.5313 × 0.7002 / tan β = 0.3720 / tan β.
tan β = 0.3720 / 1.15 = 0.3235 ⇒ β = arctan(0.3235) = 17.93°.
(iii) Partially Submerged with WT at 1.5 m, Slip Plane at z = 4 m, β = 30°:
Dry/moist zone (0 to 1.5 m): ΔW₁ = 17.66 × 1.5 = 26.49 kPa.
Submerged zone (1.5 to 4 m): ΔW₂ = 20.93 × 2.5 = 52.33 kPa.
Total vertical stress σv = 26.49 + 52.33 = 78.82 kPa.
Pore water pressure u = 9.81 × 2.5 × cos² 30° = 24.53 × 0.75 = 18.40 kPa.
Normal effective stress σ' = σv cos² 30° - u = (78.82 × 0.75) - 18.40 = 59.12 - 18.40 = 40.72 kPa.
Shear stress τ = σv sin 30° cos 30° = 78.82 × 0.5 × 0.866 = 34.13 kPa.
Available Factor of Safety: FS = σ' tan φ / τ = (40.72 × tan 35°) / 34.13 = (40.72 × 0.7002) / 34.13 = 28.51 / 34.13 = 0.835 (Unstable!).

topic: Terzaghi's Bearing Capacity Theory: Assumptions & Factors Affecting Bearing Capacity
question: List the assumptions made in Terzaghi's analysis of bearing capacity of a continuous footing.
solution:
Assumptions of Terzaghi's Bearing Capacity Theory:
1. Soil is homogeneous, isotropic, and semi-infinite.
2. Footing is a continuous strip with infinite length (L/B → ∞), forming a two-dimensional plane-strain condition.
3. Foundation is shallow, with depth of embedment Df ≤ width of footing B.
4. Base of the footing is rough, preventing soil slipping along the contact surface.
5. Soil above the foundation base level is replaced by an equivalent surcharge q = γDf (shear resistance above base level is neglected).
6. General shear failure occurs in the supporting soil mass.
7. Soil behaves as a rigid-plastic material obeying Mohr-Coulomb failure criterion (τ = c + σ tanφ).

topic: Terzaghi's Bearing Capacity Theory: Assumptions & Factors Affecting Bearing Capacity
question: Discuss the various factors that affect the bearing capacity of a shallow footing.
solution:
Factors Affecting Bearing Capacity of a Shallow Footing:
1. Shear Strength of Soil (c and φ): Higher cohesion and higher angle of internal friction increase bearing capacity factors exponentially.
2. Footing Width (B): In granular soils (sand), bearing capacity increases linearly with footing width (0.5 γ B Nγ).
3. Depth of Embedment (Df): Deeper footing placement increases the confining surcharge pressure (γ Df Nq), directly increasing bearing capacity.
4. Water Table Location: When groundwater rises to the foundation level, submerged unit weight (γ') replaces γ, reducing bearing capacity by up to 50%.
5. Shape of Footing: Circular and square footings have higher bearing capacities per unit area than continuous strip footings due to 3D shape factors.
6. Unit Weight of Soil (γ): Denser soil with higher unit weight provides greater resistance to shear displacement.

Terzaghi square footing (c = 0):
qult = γ Df Nq + 0.4 γ B Nγ = (20 × 1.0 × 7.4) + (0.4 × 20 × 1.5 × 5.0) = 148.0 + 60.0 = 208.0 kN/m².

topic: Functions and Classification of Pile Foundations
question: Explain the function of pile foundation.
solution:
Functions of Pile Foundation:
1. End-Bearing Load Transfer: Transfers heavy building loads through weak, compressible top layers down to deep stiff soil or solid bedrock.
2. Skin Friction Load Transfer: Distributes structural loads along the surface area of the pile shaft by friction in deep uniform clay or sand strata.
3. Resisting Uplift Forces: Anchors tall structures (transmission towers, chimneys, transmission masts) against upward tension and wind overturning moments.
4. Resisting Lateral Loads: Resists horizontal lateral forces caused by wind, earthquakes, earth pressures, and water wave impacts on bridge piers and docks.
5. Soil Compaction: Compaction piles densify loose granular deposits, increasing bearing capacity and mitigating earthquake liquefaction risk.

topic: Bearing Capacity Computation: Shallow vs Deep Foundations (Skin Friction vs End Bearing Mechanisms)
question: Discuss the basic difference in the bearing capacity computation of shallow and deep foundations.
solution:
Differences in Bearing Capacity Computation of Shallow and Deep Foundations:
1. Load Transfer Mechanism: Shallow foundations carry load through base contact bearing pressure only (qu), whereas deep foundations (piles) carry load through both base resistance (Qb) and shaft skin friction (Qs).
2. Surcharge Pressure: In shallow foundations, surcharge is taken as full depth q = γDf, whereas in deep foundations, effective vertical stress increases only up to a critical depth (10d to 20d) and then stays constant.
3. Bearing Capacity Factors: Shallow foundations use Terzaghi factors (e.g., Nc = 5.7 for strip footing in clay), whereas deep foundations use deep cavity expansion factors (e.g., Nc* = 9.0 per Skempton).
4. Failure Surface Extent: Shallow foundation failure planes extend outwards and upwards all the way to ground surface with visible heave, whereas pile failure surfaces are localized around the pile tip and shaft without ground heaving.
5. Settlement Influence: Shallow foundations are often governed and restricted by settlement criteria, whereas deep foundations mobilize high load capacity at small settlements.

Qsafe_friction = Qs / FS = 534.40 / 3.0 = 178.13 kN.

topic: Single Pile Static Ultimate Load Capacity in Sand Deposit (Qu = Qb + Qs, phi = 40 deg)
question: A 12 m long, 300 mm diameter pile is driven in a uniform deposit of sand (φ = 40°). The water table is at a great depth and is not likely to rise. The average dry unit weight of sand is 18 kN/m³. Using N<sub>q</sub> = 137, calculate the safe load capacity of the pile with a factor of safety of 2.5.
solution:
Given Parameters:
L = 12 m, d = 0.30 m, γ = 18 kN/m³, φ = 40°, Nq = 137, FS = 2.5.
1. Base Resistance (Qb):
Base area Ab = (π/4)(0.3)² = 0.07068 m².
Critical depth in dense sand: Lc ≈ 15 d = 15(0.3) = 4.5 m (or 20 d = 6.0 m).
At critical depth Lc = 15 d = 4.5 m, effective overburden reaches limiting value:
σ'v = γ · Lc = 18 × 4.5 = 81.0 kPa.
Limiting unit base resistance: qb = σ'v · Nq = 81.0 × 137 = 11,097 kPa.
Qb = qb · Ab = 11,097 × 0.07068 = 784.3 kN.
2. Shaft Resistance (Qs):
For φ = 40°, earth pressure coefficient K ≈ 1.0, wall friction δ ≈ 0.75 φ = 30°.
Average vertical stress along shaft from 0 to 4.5 m: σv1 = 0.5(81) = 40.5 kPa.
Average vertical stress from 4.5 to 12 m (capped): σv2 = 81.0 kPa.
fs1 = K σv1 tan δ = 1.0(40.5) tan 30° = 23.38 kPa over As1 = π(0.3)(4.5) = 4.241 m² ⇒ Qs1 = 99.1 kN.
fs2 = K σv2 tan δ = 1.0(81.0) tan 30° = 46.76 kPa over As2 = π(0.3)(7.5) = 7.068 m² ⇒ Qs2 = 330.5 kN.
Total skin friction: Qs = 99.1 + 330.5 = 429.6 kN.
3. Total Safe Capacity:
Qu = Qb + Qs = 784.3 + 429.6 = 1213.9 kN.
Qsafe = Qu / FS = 1213.9 / 2.5 = 485.56 kN.

question: A square group of 9 piles was driven into soft clay extending to a large depth. The diameter and length of the piles were 30 cm and 9 m respectively. If the unconfined compression strength of the clay is 90 kN/m², and the pile spacing is 90 cm centre to centre. Calculate the capacity of the pile group? Given Parameters:

Single pile: Qu = 9(45)(0.07068) + 0.75(45)(8.482) = 28.63 + 286.28 = 314.91 kN.

Block width B = 2s + d = 2(0.9) + 0.3 = 2.1 m.

3. Governing Capacity:
Governing ultimate Qug = min(2834.2, 5188.05) = 2834.2 kN.
Safe capacity = 2834.2 / 2.5 = 1133.68 kN.

topic: Laboratory and Field Tests for Soil Investigation Work
question: List the laboratory and field tests used for the soil investigation work.
solution:
Laboratory and Field Tests in Soil Investigation:
1. Field (In-Situ) Tests:
• Standard Penetration Test (SPT): Determines N-value, relative density of sands, and consistency of clays.
• Cone Penetration Test (CPT): Measures point resistance and sleeve friction continuously with depth.
• Plate Load Test (PLT): Evaluates ultimate bearing capacity and settlement of footings in-situ.
• Field Vane Shear Test: Determines in-situ undrained shear strength of soft cohesive soils.
2. Laboratory Tests:
• Grain Size Analysis: Sieve analysis and hydrometer test for soil classification.
• Atterberg Limits: Liquid limit and plastic limit tests to determine soil plasticity.
• Shear Strength Tests: Direct shear box test and triaxial shear test (UU, CU, CD) to find c and φ.
• Consolidation Test: Oedometer test to determine compression index and rate of settlement.

topic: Objectives & Purpose of Geotechnical Soil Exploration / Investigation
question: Describe the purpose of soil investigation.
solution:
Purpose of Soil Investigation:
1. Foundation Selection: To determine the most suitable, safe, and economical type and depth of foundation for the proposed structure.
2. Bearing Capacity Evaluation: To calculate the safe bearing capacity of soil to prevent shear failure under building loads.
3. Settlement Prediction: To estimate total and differential settlements and ensure they remain within permissible structural limits.
4. Earth Pressure Assessment: To provide design parameters (Ka, Kp) for retaining walls, basement walls, and temporary shoring.
5. Groundwater Observation: To locate the groundwater table and its seasonal fluctuations, identifying dewatering and waterproofing requirements.
6. Construction Risk Mitigation: To identify problematic soils (expansive Black Cotton soil, collapsible soils, high water seepage) before construction begins.

topic: Soil Sampler Criteria: Area Ratio (Ar), Clearance Ratios (Ci, Co) & Recovery Ratio
question: Calculate the area ratio of a thin walled tube sampler having an external diameter of 6 cm and a wall thickness of 2.25 mm. Do you recommend the sampler for obtaining undisturbed soil samples? Why?
solution:
Given: External diameter D2 = 6.0 cm = 60.0 mm, Wall thickness t = 2.25 mm.
1. Internal Diameter (D1):
D1 = D2 - 2t = 60.0 - 2(2.25) = 60.0 - 4.5 = 55.5 mm.
2. Area Ratio (Ar):
Ar = [ (D2² - D1²) / D1² ] × 100%
D2² = 60² = 3600 mm², D1² = 55.5² = 3080.25 mm².
Ar = [ (3600 - 3080.25) / 3080.25 ] × 100% = [ 519.75 / 3080.25 ] × 100% = 16.87%.
3. Recommendation & Justification:
Recommendation: Yes, this sampler is acceptable for obtaining good quality undisturbed samples in cohesive soils. Per IS: 1892, an area ratio ≤ 10% is ideal for extremely sensitive soils, but Ar up to 20% is permissible in normal medium-to-stiff clays. Because 16.87% < 20%, minimal soil displacement occurs, keeping perimeter edge disturbance low.

topic: Methods of Subsoil Exploration (Boring, Sounding, Trial Pits, Geophysical)
question: Classify the various methods of soil exploration and mention the circumstances under which each is best situated.
solution:
Classification of Soil Exploration Methods & Circumstances:
IS: 1892
Method Description Best Suited Circumstances
1. Open Test Pits Shallow manual or backhoe excavation (up to 3-5 m). Shallow foundation sites; enables direct visual inspection and block sampling.
2. Auger Boring Hand or power auger turned into ground. Cohesive clays and silts above water table (up to 10-15 m depth).
3. Wash Boring Water jet chops soil inside casing. Sands and soft clays below water table; unsuitable for rock.
4. Rotary Core Drilling Rotating diamond core barrel with drilling mud. Medium to hard rock and boulders; recovers continuous rock cores (RQD).
5. Percussion Drilling Heavy drill bit dropped repeatedly to crush soil. Bouldery, stony ground and hard glacial till.
6. Geophysical Methods Seismic refraction and electrical resistivity. Rapid preliminary reconnaissance of large sites (highways, dams, pipelines).
